claim_text: An unauthorized party got into Together AI's stored prompt samples
summary: Together AI says an unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples from its serverless inference service after a credential was exposed.
detail: This is the company's own statement, published Nov 21. It calls the event a security incident and apologizes.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Together AI's own post says an unauthorized party obtained the credential and downloaded the stored samples.

claim_text: A credential committed by an AI coding agent opened a private repository
summary: Together AI says an AI coding agent committed a credential for a private Hugging Face repository to its public GitHub repository, and the unauthorized party used it.
detail: The company says its automated scanning caught the credential and it reverted the commit. It does not say how long the credential was exposed.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The company's post describes the committed credential and the download.

claim_text: The samples were test prompts from June and July 2026
summary: Together AI says the stored samples came from requests to three models, mainly on June 24, July 4, July 8 and July 14, 2026.
detail: The company says it collected prompt samples authorized for routine software testing and stored them in a private repository. The models named are MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The company states the dates, models and purpose of the stored samples.

claim_text: The party searched the prompts for credentials and tested them
summary: Together AI says the unauthorized party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested whether they worked.
detail: Five of the credentials tested were canary credentials (fake bait keys) from a security experiment run by Dragos. The company does not say whether any real customer credentials were tested or used.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The company's post describes the searching and testing, and the five canary credentials.

claim_text: Whether the downloaded data was deleted or shared further
summary: Together AI's post first said it had no reason to believe the party leaked the data further and understood it had been deleted. That sentence is gone from the post as updated at 12:56 AM ET on Nov 22.
detail: The company has not said why it removed the sentence. No public source now says whether the data was deleted or passed on. Some news reports, including The Hacker News, still repeat the original line.
label: Not established
why_it_supports: The archived copy of the post shows the sentence; the current post does not.
notes: Label changed from Reported on Nov 22 after the company edited its post.

claim_text: Together AI worked with outside forensics and law enforcement
summary: Together AI says an external forensic investigation firm and law enforcement are involved, and it found no evidence of other prompt leakage.
detail: Its review of the affected prompts is ongoing, to see whether personal or other customer data was exposed.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The company's post says so in its own words.

claim_text: Which customers were affected, and what was in the prompts
summary: Together AI says it is still reviewing the prompts to decide which customers to notify directly.
detail: Neither the number of customers nor the number of prompts has been published.
label: Not established
why_it_supports: The company says the review is ongoing and gives no counts.

claim_text: Together AI's advice: turn on zero data retention
summary: Together AI tells customers with sensitive prompts to turn on zero data retention (ZDR) in account settings, and says ZDR is now the default for new accounts.
detail: It also lists scoped or short-lived credentials, credential checks on all pull requests and new rules for AI coding agents.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The company lists these steps in its post.

claim_text: A researcher's canary test found other AI providers compromised
summary: Dragos says it sent about two million prompts with fake credentials to AI services and saw evidence that data from at least three AI providers was exposed.
detail: Dragos does not name the three providers in the part we read. Ars Technica reports the same finding. We cannot tell from public sources whether Together AI is one of the three, though Together says five of the credentials the intruder tested were Dragos canaries.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Dragos describes its findings, and Ars Technica and The Hacker News independently report them.

claim_text: Together AI's incident is the one Dragos's research traced
summary: Together AI says five tested credentials were Dragos canaries, so the Dragos research is linked to this incident by the company's own words.
detail: No source says whether the Dragos research is how Together AI learned of the incident.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: Together names Dragos canaries; Dragos does not name Together in the text we read.

claim_text: OpenRouter dropped three providers and pulled 125 endpoints from its zero-data-retention list
summary: OpenRouter says it off-boarded three providers, removed 125 endpoints from zero data retention (ZDR) eligibility, and notified all potentially affected customers.
detail: OpenRouter does not name the three providers in its post. The Hacker News reports that neither Dragos nor OpenRouter has said whether OpenRouter's three are the same as Dragos's three.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: OpenRouter's own post states the actions, and The Hacker News reports them.

claim_text: OpenRouter says it was not breached
summary: OpenRouter says the researchers' findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter itself.
detail: The findings concern providers that sit behind OpenRouter. OpenRouter's list of provider notices now links Atlas Cloud, Novita, Phala and Together; Atlas Cloud was added on Nov 22.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: OpenRouter's own statement, with no outside check.

claim_text: Phala and Novita have posted their own notices
summary: Phala says an attacker got into its systems and request data for one model was exposed for requests from Oct 21 to Nov 8. Novita says a routing error sent some MiniMax requests to MiniMax's own API from May 28 to Nov 11.
detail: These are separate incidents with different causes. Novita says the pattern suggests automated content review, not an attack. Together AI's cause (an exposed credential) is different from both.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Each company's own notice states its cause and window.

claim_text: Whether one attacker is behind all of these incidents
summary: Phala says a single actor did both of its intrusions. No source links the Together AI intruder to Phala's attacker or anyone else.
detail: Dragos and Ars Technica say two of the three compromised providers were probably hit by the same adversary, but do not say which providers.
label: Not established
why_it_supports: No source names the Together AI intruder or ties it to another incident.

claim_text: Atlas Cloud says MiniMax's own API was where prompts were opened, and pulled its models from OpenRouter
summary: Atlas Cloud says a researcher's tests showed a third party opening prompts sent to MiniMax's official API, not on Atlas Cloud's own systems. It stopped sending requests there and emailed affected accounts.
detail: The requests went through Atlas Cloud in the third and early fourth quarter of 2026. Atlas Cloud says it chose to take every one of its models off OpenRouter while it tests them, and that this was its decision, not OpenRouter's. It does not say whether it is one of the three providers OpenRouter off-boarded. Its finding about MiniMax is its own account of the researcher's tests; we found no MiniMax statement. Together AI's samples also include MiniMax M3 requests, but Together's cause (an exposed credential) is different.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Atlas Cloud's own notice states its actions and its account of the tests, and OpenRouter's list links it.
notes: Atlas Cloud's statements about its own actions are Confirmed; the MiniMax finding rests on Atlas Cloud's account of the researcher's tests.
